options.label: A
options.text: Bromide first removes H⁺ from the alkene

options.label: B
options.text: HBr adds through homolytic cleavage only

options.label: C
options.text: Protonation leading to a secondary carbocation is favoured over the primary alternative

options.label: D
options.text: The main product must be chiral

questions.answerSummary: The secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary carbocation. Bromide attacks the more commonly formed intermediate.

steps.text: The secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary carbocation. Bromide attacks the more commonly formed intermediate.

questions.title: Competing kinetic models
questions.stem:
The table gives constructed initial rates for A+B→products. A calibrated optical probe tracks a product whose absorbance is linear in concentration. Temperature is constant within each run. Rate units are mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹; concentrations are mol dm⁻³.

| Run | T / K | [A] | [B] | Initial rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 300 | 0.100 | 0.100 | 0.000500 |
| 2 | 300 | 0.200 | 0.100 | 0.00200 |
| 3 | 300 | 0.200 | 0.200 | 0.00400 |
| 4 | 315 | 0.100 | 0.100 | 0.00100 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine both partial orders and the rate expression at 300 K.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate k at 300 K, give its units, and predict the initial rate at [A]=0.150 and [B]=0.0800 at 300 K.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Use runs 1 and 4 to estimate Ea. Use R=8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and assume the rate law and Arrhenius prefactor apply over this range.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Assess the claim that the rate law proves a single elementary three-particle collision. Suggest how to reduce bias when extracting initial rates.

steps.text: Runs 1 and 2: doubling A at fixed B quadruples rate, so order in A is two.
Runs 2 and 3: doubling B at fixed A doubles rate, so order in B is one.
rate=k[A]²[B].
For total order three, units are dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.
Concentrations match, so k₃₁₅/k₃₀₀=2.00.
Ea≈36.3 kJ mol⁻¹.
Overall kinetic orders do not by themselves establish a unique mechanism.
A fast pre-equilibrium before a slower elementary step can produce the same concentration dependence.
Acquire many early-time points and estimate the initial tangent before significant reactant depletion; accept a justified fitting procedure.

questions.title: Equilibrium by absorbance
questions.stem: Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ ⇌ FeSCN²⁺. A calibration for FeSCN²⁺ has intercept 0.025 and slope 5000 dm³ mol⁻¹. At the chosen wavelength other species give negligible absorbance after background correction. Initial concentrations in the final mixture are 1.000×10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ Fe³⁺ and 8.00×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ SCN⁻. Initial complex concentration is zero. The equilibrium absorbance is 0.925.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the calibration to determine the equilibrium complex concentration. Explain why the intercept must be used.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate both remaining reactant concentrations and Kc using equilibrium concentrations in mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Water doubles the volume at the same temperature. Compare the immediate Qc with Kc and predict the subsequent change in complex amount.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why a lower absorbance immediately after dilution does not, by itself, prove a shift. Design one comparison that isolates the shift.

steps.text: A=0.025+5000c; net complex signal is 0.900.
Ignoring the positive background assigns excess absorbance to the complex and overestimates its concentration.
1:1 consumption leaves [Fe³⁺]=8.20×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³.
[SCN⁻]=6.20×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³.
Kc=[complex]/([Fe³⁺][SCN⁻])≈354 using the stated concentration convention.
All three concentrations initially halve.
Qc increases by (1/2)/(1/2)²=2, so Qc=2Kc.
The reaction shifts left, decreasing the amount of complex from its immediate post-dilution value.
Dilution alone halves the complex concentration before chemical re-equilibration.
For pure dilution the predicted absorbance is 0.025+0.900/2=0.475 if background is unchanged.
Compare final equilibrated absorbance with 0.475 using matched blanks and the same path length; a lower net signal supports further dissociation.

questions.title: Locating a weak-acid endpoint
questions.stem:
A 25.00 cm³ aliquot of HA is titrated with 0.1000 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 298 K. Equivalence volume is 20.00 cm³, the pH there is 8.7, and the steep region spans pH 7.6–10.0. Assume volumes are additive and neglect activity effects.

| NaOH added / cm³ | 5.00 | 10.00 | 15.00 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Measured pH | 4.32 | 4.80 | 5.28 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the original analytical concentration of HA and derive pKa from the half-equivalence reading.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the conjugate pair ratio, predict the pH at 15.00 cm³ and compare with the reading.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Indicator M changes at pH 3.1–4.4 and N at 8.2–10.0. Choose an indicator and explain the basic equivalence pH.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: At 10.00 cm³ the buffer is diluted twofold with water. Predict both its approximate pH and its buffer capacity per unit volume. State a limit to the pH prediction.

steps.text: The 1:1 endpoint corresponds to 0.1000×0.02000=0.002000 mol HA.
At 10.00 cm³ equal amounts HA and A⁻ give pH=pKa=4.80.
OH⁻ forms 1.500 mmol A⁻ and leaves 0.500 mmol HA.
pH=pKa+log₁₀(3)=5.28.
The prediction agrees within the displayed precision, supporting the buffer model in this region.
Choose N because its transition lies within the steep section.
The conjugate base A⁻ reacts with water: A⁻+H₂O⇌HA+OH⁻.
The HA:A⁻ ratio is unchanged, so pH remains about 4.80.
Both buffer concentrations halve; capacity per unit volume decreases.
At very large dilution, ionization of water and changes in dissociation can invalidate the simple concentration-ratio approximation.
